title: Priming entropy maplet runlog (scratch)
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for the "entropy maplet" idea — small experiment harness to map how priming (prefix tokens) and request entropy interact with warm/cold cache behaviour and batching. I ran a focused sweep on a dev-gpu pool (a2-medium-ish approximator VM) to get actionable p95/p99 numbers and a feel for thresholds where batching hurts tail.

Test setup (notes):
- cluster: dev-fleet-a (4×A100-sim nodes, dev profile, logging to /tmp/priming-maplet)
- model: open-small-v2 (ca. 7B equivalent, kv-cache enabled)
- route config: single-instance no autoscale, steady qps driver
- harness: local python bench harness that can vary: concurrency, client-batch-size, priming-length, entropy-temp
- measurement window: 20k requests per run (5 warmup buckets of 2k + 3 measurement buckets of 4k)
- metric collection: token-level timing + request end-to-end (client entry -> first token -> last token)

Parameters swept (discrete):
- priming_length_tokens: [0, 8, 32, 128]
- client_batch_size (pack multiple prompt requests into one GPU batch, offloader): [1, 4, 16]
- concurrency (in-flight requests): [8, 32, 128]
- temperature: [0.2, 0.8] (low/high entropy)
- cache_state: [cold (after restart), warm (after 2k warm requests), primed (explicitly prefilled with same prefix)]

Representative results (condensed):
Run id: MAP-20260312-A (priming=32, batch=4, conc=32, temp=0.8, warm)
- p50: 38 ms (E2E)
- p95: 160 ms
- p99: 450 ms
- throughput: 620 qps sustained (measured tokens/sec normalized)
- kv-cache hit-rate: 0.72 (prefix cache only)
- notes: visible tail spikes aligned to coalesced batch flush events (client batch timer occasionally held tiny bursts -> big latency outliers)

Run id: MAP-20260312-B (priming=128, batch=16, conc=128, temp=0.2, cold)
- p50: 120 ms
- p95: 920 ms
- p99: 1.9 s
- throughput: 1,100 qps peak then collapsed to ~400 qps under sustained traffic (queueing/backpressure)
- kv-cache hit-rate: 0.18 (cold)
- notes: long priming increases KV insertion cost; cold-start combined with large batches amplifies tail. Memory churn on device visible in metrics.

Small ascii sparkline of p99 across priming lengths (batch=4, conc=32, temp=0.8):
priming 0   |########                               | p99 ~ 210ms
priming 8   |#####                                  | p99 ~ 170ms
priming 32  |###                                    | p99 ~ 160ms
priming 128 |##########################             | p99 ~ 700ms

Quick hypotheses & observations: 
1) Low-to-moderate priming (8-32 tokens) tends to *reduce* tail for warm caches at moderate concurrency — the runtime amortizes KV-cache hits and avoids repeated attention re-setup for short contexts.
2) Long priming (>=128 tokens) creates device memory churn and larger kernel launches -> hurts tail, especially when combined with large client-side batches. 
3) High entropy (temp=0.8) slightly increases p50/p95 but doesn't change the qualitative trend; tails are more sensitive to batching behavior than sampling randomness.
4) Cold cache + large client batches is the worst case: the batching timer causes request pileups and long queueing + large kernel launches.
5) Explicit "primed" state (prefill identical prefix) yields best p99, but priming content matters (if prefix is diverse, cache effectiveness drops).

Anomalies seen: 
- Intermittent spikes that correlate with pod GC-like memory reclamation (see node metrics) at ~15:42 UTC — investigating whether runtime schedule triggered a cleanup during high concurrency.
- One run showed throughput oscillation (1.1k -> 400 qps). Root cause looks like async queue backlog + backpressure; need trace-level correlation.

Next quick experiments (TODOs):
- Re-run narrow sweep with client-batch timer tuned (0ms / 5ms / 20ms) to see coalescing impact on p99. Link to ticket JIRA-INFR-4123.
- Add per-kernel-launch time instrumentation (PR 742 references instrumentation scaffold).
- Test with dedicated smaller-quantized model variant to see whether kernel overheads dominate priming cost.
- Try prefetching KV for frequent prefixes (simulate multi-tenant hot prefixes) and measure eviction interactions.

Actionable short-term ops recommendations (for proto):
- For medium-latency SLO routes, limit client-side batch size to <=4 and prefer priming <=32 tokens.
- Introduce a bounded batching timer that favors immediate flush under high concurrency (experiment: 1ms flush).
- Add telemetry: sample trace-level spans for kernel launches and cache-insert operations to pinpoint memory churn.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- "entropy maplet" naming: map axes = priming_length (x), client_batch_size (y), measured p99 (z) and color by cache state. Good canvas for a small viz in bench-dashboard.
- Share distilled result with Derek + Maya tomorrow; ask infra for a repeat on dedicated QA pool.
- Link bench script: ~/repos/bench/entropy-maplet/runner.py (diff pending).

References & links inside:
- bench runner PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench/pull/31
- infra issue: JIRA-INFR-4123 (priming vs batching tail)
- runtime instrumentation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/742

End of scratchpad — keep this raw. Will extract short findings into a one-pager if results hold on QA cluster.

-- Kiera
